TEN DAYS OUT — Review Panel
Manuscript read in full: 32,261 words, 10 chapters. Ratings and notes below are from the text as written, not the brief.
ROUND 1 — INDEPENDENT REVIEWS
1. THE KU READER — ★★★★☆ (4/5)
Verdict: Finished it in one sitting and would pick up Book 2 — but I'd review it as "steamy," not "spicy," and the publisher shouldn't tell me otherwise.
Three biggest strengths
Beth. She is the rare suspense heroine who is good at her actual job and it matters. Ch.1 (the dead reefer unit, the sprung lid, photographing the plate low at her hip) sells her in ten pages. In danger she counts, checks, withholds — the Ch.4 beat where she sits on the gait identification for a day until she's seen the walk twice is exactly right.
The island as a machine. Barometer, tides, check-in net, bank bag, float lights on a timer. By Ch.9 I believed the trap because I'd been taught the boat for eight chapters — the 34 steps, the binder she'd put his hand on, the floods going dark as a signal.
The midpoint. Ch.5: the shed fire, the bar crossing at knee-to-thigh depth with her fist in his belt, then the fish house. Best chapter in the book. Suspense and heat in the same movement.
Three biggest problems
The heat is a 3, not a 3–4. Ch.5 is hands-only. Ch.6 and Ch.8 are frank in vocabulary ("clit," "cock," condoms handled honestly — good) but short and literary rather than sensory; each scene resolves in a page or two and cuts to aftermath. Against genre heat-4 — Lora Leigh, Maya Banks territory — this reads one full level cooler. The emotional charge is high; the explicit charge is not.
Ch.6 sags. Three days (Tue–Thu) compressed into one chapter, and the middle is errands: store, float, kindling. I skimmed the Ch.4 generator bleed-out (we'd already had a generator priming scene in Ch.3, same counting, same diesel knuckles) and the Ch.5-end paint-can suspect list, which recaps what I already knew.
She forgives the notebook too fast. Ch.7 is a gut-punch — ASSESS… Do not disclose to subject, the $9,000 known since Saturday. By Ch.8 afternoon they're in the bunk. I believed her reasons (the fish house wasn't in the book) but I wanted one night of her not touching him before the daylight scene. The speed cost the Ch.8 scene some of its power.
Where I'd have stopped: Nowhere — no DNF point. Skims as above.
Change first: Pick a lane on heat. Either lengthen Ch.6/Ch.8 on the page, or market this honestly as steamy heat-3 and let the suspense carry it.
2. THE DEVELOPMENTAL EDITOR — ★★★½ (3.5/5)
Verdict: Structurally the most competent AI-drafted romance I've seen — planted, paid off, correctly shaped — with its failures concentrated exactly where structure can't help: one character's moral logic and one forgiveness that arrives a day early.
Three biggest strengths
Plant/payoff discipline. The sticking latch (Ch.2) identifies the intruder as a stranger. The float-light timer (Ch.6) aborts the extraction (Ch.7). The binder walk-through before dark (Ch.9) is the climax mechanism. Nothing is decoration; everything is load-bearing.
Midpoint and dark moment are real. Ch.5 fire flips the book from hiding to hunting. Ch.7 notebook reframes every prior kindness as possible handling — and the reframing is fair, because the reader heard "She doesn't know" (Ch.3) and "I'll ask her" (Ch.4) alongside Beth.
Beth's arc is thematic, not decorative. Counter/checklists → choosing the ground, the radio, and her own voice in Ch.9 ("I'm alone. On the boat. Tonight." — a lie built entirely of truths she selected). Dane's mirror arc (rules → reported himself) is thinner but present.
On the leak: I wrote "Tess" in the margin in Ch.3 — the spiral log sitting open by the register plus the booster making her store the island's only working phone is a loud combination. I was certain in Ch.6, at "your office coordinated with local emergency management for the landing" — she'd been named emergency management director back in Ch.2. That's ~55% for certainty, confirmation at Ch.8. Suspicion at 55% is correct timing for this genre; Dane's nightly calls keep a live alternative running, so it plays fair. It is not too early — but it means the last 45% runs on dramatic irony, and Ch.6–7 aren't built to exploit that (Beth is still solving; the reader is waiting for her to catch up).
Three biggest problems
Tess's culpability doesn't reconcile. Leaking under pressure from a $1,800/month tank loan is one character. Planting $9,000 in Beth's account to impeach her (Ch.7/10) is a colder, more deliberate act — and "they said they'd only scare you" doesn't cover it. Then the ending treats her gently (cuff clear of the bruise, the saltines, "Make Ned eat something"). Either the frame-up needs to be the smugglers' plant via her bag without her knowledge, or her ending needs to be less forgiven.
The dark-moment repair is under-built. One crew-mess conversation (Ch.8) carries: six days of withheld material fact, a professional assessment log, and a sexual relationship. Her checkable proof — that he kept the fish house out of the book — happens in her head at 6:40am before the conversation. Give the verification a scene and a cost, or delay the reconciliation.
The final page. Quist handing Russ the envelope ("Three harbors. One account.") in the last 300 words: I could not tell whether Russ is being recruited, warned, or accused. A hook should open a question; this one opens a confusion, and it retrospectively dirties the man who arrested Arsenault and saved Tess.
Change first: Fix Tess. Every other problem is revision; this one is a character who currently commits two different crimes for two different people.
3. THE LINE EDITOR / AI-PROSE SPOTTER — ★★★☆ (3/5)
Verdict: Sentence by sentence this is well above machine-average — but it is identifiable as machine-written within two chapters, not by errors, by regularity.
Strengths: genuine work-detail vocabulary (binder handles, D-rings, Generac priming) that never sounds researched-at-you; dialogue tags kept clean; a controlled motif system (counting, hands, doors) that mostly earns its repetitions.
Recurring tics, with chapters
Enumeration as a nervous system. 14 cartons (Ch.1), 11 ladder rungs (Ch.1), barometer tapped five times with readings marching 1000→986 (Ch.1–2), 340 steps counted four times (Ch.3–6), 22 boats (Ch.4), primer strokes counted to 38 and later 30 (Ch.3, Ch.4). Once is character. This often is a metronome.
Signature phrases on loop. "Put it where she put the things…" (Ch.1, with variants Ch.2, Ch.7). Objects "squared" to edges — ledgers, notebooks, bags — nine times. Wheelhouse smelling of "burnt coffee and wet wool" three times (Ch.1, Ch.8, Ch.10), nearly verbatim.
Characters reduced to one tic each. Ned switches his hearing aid off (7 mentions). Russ takes his cap off, looks into it, puts it back (3 times, same wording). Dane's "right side clear" (Ch.2, 4, 5). Tess tugs the braid. The tics are eventually used as clues — but a human writer varies the surface even when the tell is fixed.
Sentence shape. Average ~11 words; roughly one sentence in five is a four-words-or-fewer fragment. Long runs of "Then he… / She didn't…" (78 instances of "He didn't," 39 of "She didn't," 14 of "didn't ask"). Scene after scene ends on the same cadence — a withheld action in a short final line: "She didn't step out" (Ch.2), "His pen was still moving" (Ch.4), "She was keeping an exit again" (Ch.7).
Duplicate scene engineering. The generator repair is staged twice as an intimacy set-piece (Ch.3 shed, Ch.4 shed) with near-identical choreography: count the primer, diesel in the knuckles, bodies too close in a gap "barely a body wide."
Do the leads sound like different people? No. Beth and Dane share one register — clipped, procedural, aphoristic, fond of defining by negation ("That's not no. Not with that door open behind me"). Dane's Lowell backstory (Ch.4) is good material delivered in Beth's exact cadence. Tess is the only fully distinct voice in the book; Ned and Russ are separable mainly by which tic they perform.
Change first: A human pass whose only job is de-regularisation — break the counting habit in half the scenes, vary each tic's wording, and let Dane think in a different sentence length than Beth.
4. THE KDP MARKET STRATEGIST — ★★★½ (3.5/5)
Verdict: A viable series asset and a weak standalone product. The brief's central tension — PG-13 packaging, heat 3–4 interior — is where the money leaks.
Fit and length. The book delivers Romantic Suspense expectations cleanly: protector hero, witness heroine, isolated setting, HEA, case closed. At 32k words it will normalise to roughly 150–190 KU pages — call it ~$0.65–$0.85 for a complete read at recent KENP rates. At $2.99 (70% royalty ≈ $2.09) one purchase is worth ~3 full KU reads, and standalone Amazon ads at genre CPCs will not pay back on a single novella. 30,000 words is not a quality problem; it is a unit-economics problem. It is solved only by read-through: Book 2 available or on preorder at launch, Books 2–3 inside 30–45 days.
The packaging mismatch is the biggest commercial risk. A clothed, stormy-ferry cover is normal for this category and won't trip adult filtering — filtering is driven by cover, title/subtitle and erotic keywords, not interior heat. But a blurb written to PG-13 that never signals steam, fronted by a manuscript whose own opening note announces "on-page sex," sets two traps: clean-romance browsers who sample it will leave "explicit, not as advertised" reviews, and spice readers who'd love it will never click. Signal the heat in the blurb ("steamy," "open door") while keeping the cover clean. Do not use "witness protection programme" keywords — the book is explicit that she is not in the programme ("You're in the waiting room for the programme"), and mismatched metadata draws its own complaints.
Launch plan: $2.99, KU-exclusive, subtitle carrying "A Cutter Island Romantic Suspense Novella"; categories Romantic Suspense + Small Town Romance + Law Enforcement Romance; Book 2 preorder live on day one; spend nothing on ads until Book 2 exists, then advertise Book 1 against series LTV; ARC to romantic-suspense readers, not clean-romance lists. Front matter: replace [PEN NAME], and keep the content note — it's well written and it does the expectation-setting the blurb should share.
Change first: Don't launch it alone. The book is a funnel entry, and should be published like one.
5. THE SKEPTIC — ★★½ (2.5/5)
Verdict: This is a competent simulation of a romantic suspense novella by a pipeline that has learned what every beat is for — and the strongest reason not to publish it as-is is that a reader who detects that will feel handled, not told a story.
Strengths (being fair): Beth's competence is specific, not "feisty heroine" wallpaper. The Ch.9 trap is genuinely well built. The prose has no howlers.
Three biggest problems
Everybody is a mechanism. Each islander carries exactly one secret, one debt and one tic: Beth's father's boat, Tess's tank loan, Dane's dead witness, Ned's subsidy, Russ's cousin. Real casts have waste in them. Here, nothing is wasted — and a book in which every detail pays off eventually feels engineered in a way readers describe as "soulless" without being able to name why.
The emotional arithmetic is too neat. His dead witness (ten minutes, a parking lot) is precisely the trauma required to explain precisely the choice he must make about precisely this witness. Marisol is a key cut for one lock. Beth's Ch.8 capitulation then completes the symmetry on schedule.
The disclosure problem is real, not theoretical. KDP requires AI-generated content to be disclosed at upload. Beyond compliance: this category runs on author-reader trust, pen-name intimacy, newsletters, "my characters" social posts. A pipeline book marketed as a human author's heartfelt work invites a backlash cycle that will attach to the pen name permanently if it surfaces post-launch — and prose this regular will be spotted and posted about (see the Line Editor's list; readers do this for sport now).
Change first: Decide what this pen name is, honestly, before launch — because the book's quality is good enough that people will ask, and "we hid it" is the only answer that ends the brand.
ROUND 2 — CROSS-TALK
Disagreement 1 — How damning is the notebook forgiveness?
The KU Reader and the Editor split. Reader: "He disclosed before Ch.5 — 'When this is over, I report this' — and he did report himself, at cost. That bought him most of Ch.8 for me." Editor: "He reported the relationship. The $9,000 he sat on from Saturday to Friday is the betrayal, and it's answered with 'coaching ends your testimony' — a policy, not a reckoning."
KU Reader changes her rating: 4 → 3.5. "On reflection the Editor's right that my forgiveness came from the reporting, which covers a different sin than the one that hurt."
Disagreement 2 — Was Tess too obvious?
Line Editor backs the Editor's Ch.3 margin note and adds: the tic-stacking around Tess (books squared, smoothed, squared again, Ch.6) is the prose pointing. The KU Reader dissents for the actual buying audience: "I did not clock her until Ned said 'Tess doesn't count' in Ch.8. Genre readers read at speed, at night, for the couple. The clues read as warmth until they don't." Strategist's ruling, accepted by both: for a first read at KU speed, the timing works; for reviewers and rereaders — the people who write the detailed 3-star reviews — she is solved by Ch.6.
Disagreement 3 — Is 30k words a flaw or a format?
KU Reader: "It's why I finished it. My queue is novellas." Strategist: "And it's why it can't carry ads or a $3.99 price alone. Both true. The format isn't the flaw; publishing it as a standalone is."
Skeptic changes his rating: 2.5 → 3. "The Ch.9 sequence isn't generic — the binder lesson, the ring buoy, 'It's at your head. Arm through it' — a human staff writer would be proud of that set-piece. My objection stands on disclosure and Tess, not on craft absence."
ROUND 3 — CHAIR'S SYNTHESIS
Consensus rating: 3.3/5 (KU Reader 3.5, Developmental Editor 3.5, Line Editor 3, Strategist 3.5, Skeptic 3).
Verdict: Ten Days Out is a genuinely readable, correctly engineered romantic suspense novella with an unusually competent heroine and a climax that pays off eight chapters of setup — held back from publishable by one character whose motives don't reconcile (Tess), one chapter that sags (Ch.6), one forgiveness that lands a day early, and a final page that confuses instead of hooking. Its commercial ceiling is set less by its quality than by its packaging contradiction and its length economics.
The five changes that would most improve it, ranked
Reconcile Tess. Either the $9,000 frame-up is planted through her bag without her knowledge, or her role and her ending both get colder. (Editor, Skeptic)
Earn the Ch.8 reconciliation. Put Beth's verification — the fish house's absence from his notebook — into a checkable scene, and let the daylight scene come after a visible cost to Dane, not in the same conversation as the explanation. (Editor, KU Reader)
Rebuild Ch.6. Three days in one chapter is where pace dies. Cut the second generator set-piece's twin (Ch.4) or compress Wed–Thu; give each day one new fact about the leak so the reader's Ch.6 certainty becomes tension instead of waiting. (Editor, Line Editor, KU Reader)
Clarify the Russ hook. Two lines in Ch.10 establishing whether he is recruited, compromised, or inheriting the fuel run — a question, not a muddle — or end the book on Quist's ledger line and save Russ for Book 2's opening. (All five)
Settle the heat contract. Raise Ch.6/Ch.8 to a true heat-4 or market the book as steamy heat-3 everywhere — blurb, categories, ARC lists — and drop the brief's "PG-13 packaging" instruction, which every reviewer who addressed it judged wrong. (KU Reader, Strategist, Skeptic)
Continuity and logic — checked
Cleared: The calendar is exact — Thu Nov 12 to Mon Nov 23, subpoena day, "ten days… Sunday the twenty-second" all align. Barometer sequence, Dane's left-arm injury and its restrictions, the gait/right-heel-deep boot logic, and the condom progression across the three scenes (none available → bought at the store → used) are consistently tracked.
Flagged: (a) The ferry deadheads back to Cutter on Thursday night (Ch.1), yet Dane arrives on the "eight o'clock out of Pruett" Friday (Ch.2) — the boat's overnight position flips without explanation. (b) Beth's line is dead Saturday 6:20am (Ch.3) while Ned calls the district from the store's back office the same morning — one line establishing the store line/booster as separate would close it. (c) The boot-print photograph (Ch.3) is taken, shown to Russ, and never enters the evidence chain — a dropped thread. (d) Russ's solo off-page arrest of an armed Arsenault at the store back door (Ch.9) is asserted, not made plausible. (e) Testimony in the morning, indictment by 4:10pm (Ch.10) — compressed past even genre norms; survivable, but a knowledgeable reader will note it.
Publishable? Publishable after a revision pass. Not as-is, and not unviable. Before KDP, a human must: (1) make and implement the Tess decision and the Russ ending; (2) do the Ch.6 compression and the de-regularisation line pass against the Line Editor's tic list; (3) choose the heat position and rewrite the blurb to match it; (4) complete the AI-generated-content disclosure KDP requires at upload, and decide the pen name's public stance before launch, not after; (5) hold publication until Book 2 is drafted and on preorder.
On the experiment: The pipeline's strengths are architectural — premise, planting and payoff, continuity tracking across 32,000 words, and scene-level prose with real occupational texture. Its weaknesses are exactly the ones its own simulated cold reader evidently couldn't catch, because every agent in the chain read the bible rather than the book: it cannot tell what it has actually revealed (Tess by Ch.6), what it has actually made clear (the Russ ending), or when an emotional debt has actually been paid (Ch.8). It produces homogenised voice because one model is, in effect, doing every job. The honest conclusion: this pipeline is a strong drafting engine that reliably produces a 3–3.5-star manuscript — the distance from there to a sellable 4-star book is a human editor with authority over two or three decisions, and for the next test, at least one cold reader who is given the manuscript and nothing else.
